topics.title: 13.1.1 Partitioning by Business Identity Rather Than Convenience
topics.summary: A partition key determines which operations share an authority. Choosing job ID spreads independent jobs, while choosing tenant ID keeps a tenant’s jobs together. The first may improve distribution; the second may simplify tenant-level transactions and quotas. Neither is universally correct.

topics.summary: Uniform key counts do not imply uniform resource demand. One tenant can produce most of the traffic; one job can require far more computation than another. A partition with few keys can be the bottleneck if those keys are hot or their records are large.

topics.title: 13.3.1 Defining a Migration State Machine
topics.summary: A migration needs named phases, such as prepare, copy, catch up, transfer authority, verify, and retire. The exact protocol depends on the storage system, but the sequence must explain which owner accepts writes at each point and how writes occurring during the copy are retained.

cards.question: Explain Defining a Migration State Machine in your own words.
cards.answer: A migration needs named phases, such as prepare, copy, catch up, transfer authority, verify, and retire. The exact protocol depends on the storage system, but the sequence must explain which owner accepts writes at each point and how writes occurring during the copy are retained.

topics.title: 13.3.2 Avoiding Unsafe Dual Writes and Premature Cleanup
topics.summary: Writing to both old and new stores seems like an easy migration strategy until one write succeeds and the other fails. The caller must then decide which store is authoritative, how to repair divergence, and whether to return success. Without a protocol, dual writes merely add another distributed transaction problem.

reading.title: Engineering case — Move one key while preserving a late retry
paragraphs: Key route7 belongs to shard A and has a committed receipt. A membership change assigns it to shard B. A client still holding the old map sends a retry to A, while another client with the new map sends the same retry to B.

A safe migration must define both paths. Before authority transfer, A remains the writer and B is a copy in progress. After transfer, B owns complete required state, and A rejects or forwards stale-epoch requests under a bounded protocol. There must not be an interval in which both independent stores treat the key as new.

A copy phase needs a consistent starting point and a way to account for writes during copying. If A commits an additional result after the snapshot, B must catch it up before becoming authoritative. For immutable completed receipts the copy is simpler, but pending state and other mutable metadata still require a rule.

Record a cutover revision and verify B has reached it. Then transfer authority and update routing. Delayed clients do not disappear at cutover, so A’s retained redirect or rejection state needs a lifetime compatible with client cache and request retention. Deleting A immediately may turn a recoverable stale route into an unexplained outage.

Rollback after B accepts new work is not simply routing back to A. A may now be stale. A safe rollback requires reverse synchronization or another authority transition that preserves B’s accepted state. Calling the old node a “backup” does not make it current.

The rendezvous-hash test supplies only the placement component of this story. It can identify which keys would move, but it cannot establish that their receipts arrived or that old writers were fenced. A migration plan should keep those columns separate: selected destination, copied state, caught-up revision, transferred authority, and verified retry behavior.

For a small system, stopping writes during a controlled move can avoid the complexity of online catch-up. That is a legitimate availability tradeoff when documented and tested. The unsafe choice is to claim an online migration while using a file copy that races with ongoing writes and has no cutover protocol.
